It accompanies the singing and prayer of yogis and wandering holy men, and also appears in kirtan chanting and Sufi chanting. In Nepal it can accompany recitation of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. It is usually held by a single player, and its sound supports the voice and forms a drone.

Squeezing the two sides of the neck slackens the string and lowers the pitch, and the slightest bend changes the note; there are no marks for the squeeze or the pitch, so it is set by ear. Sizes run to treble, alto and bass, and the bass type often has two strings. The ektara is a single-string plucked instrument found in Bengali traditional music and in modern Bengali and eastern Indian music, and also in Nepal. It is built with a gourd resonator covered in skin, a bamboo neck pushed through it and one finger plucking the string; the player holds it upright, grips the neck above the resonator and plucks with the index finger, and squeezing the sides of the neck slackens the string and lowers the pitch, tuned by ear. It is used in Baul music and by yogis and wandering holy men for singing and prayer, and in Nepal it accompanies the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. It belongs to the zithers / struck / keyed chordophones, H-S 314/315/316.
艾克塔拉起源於孟加拉，為包爾音樂常用一弦撥奏樂器，以葫蘆蒙皮共鳴箱插入竹頸，單指: The ektara originated in Bengal and is the one-string plucked instrument common in Baul music, with a skin-covered gourd resonator, a bamboo neck pushed through it and one finger plucking the string as a drone. The tradition of accompanying religious singing can be traced back to images in the Ajanta caves of the fourth to fifth centuries, where a singer chants to Indra with a one-string zither beside him, built like the alapini vina. It later spread to eastern India, Nepal and western India, and is used by yogis, wandering holy men and Sufi adepts, and by the Tharu, Bhil, Kokna and Warli peoples. Instruments of the same name include variants with a drum body, bamboo strips tensioning the string and struck playing; the bass instrument is often called the dotara and has two strings. In recent years pop bands and films have taken up Baul music, and Purna Das Baul has criticised them for damaging its essence.
